                                               PROJECT NO. 58000

 RULEMAKING TO UPDATE                                         §   PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 WHOLESALE AND IOU RETAIL                                     §
 TRANSMISSION COST RECOVERY IN                                §           OF TEXAS
 THE ERCOT REGION                                             §

     JOINT COMMENTS OF WIND ENERGY TRANSMISSION TEXAS, LLC;
  SHARYLAND UTILITIES, L.L.C.; CROSS TEXAS TRANSMISSION, LLC; LONE
 STAR TRANSMISSION, LLC; AND ELECTRIC TRANSMISSION TEXAS, LLC ON
THE PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION OF AMENDMENTS TO 16 TAC §§ 25.192 AND
                    25.193 AND NEW 16 TAC § 25.252

       Wind Energy Transmission Texas, LLC; Sharyland Utilities, L.L.C.; Cross Texas
Transmission, LLC, and Electric Transmission Texas, LLC (collectively, “Joint TSPs”) jointly
submit these comments on the Proposal for Publication Amendments to 16 Tex. Admin. Code §§
25.192 and 25.193 (“TAC”) and New 16 TAC § 25.252 (“PFP”).1 Per the PFP, comments are due
August 11, 2026. Therefore, these comments are timely filed.

                                         I.       Executive Summary
       The Joint TSPs appreciate the opportunity to participate in the process of revising
transmission cost allocation and rate design in the Electric Reliability Council of Texas
(“ERCOT”) area.         The Joint TSPs are all transmission-only transmission service providers
(“TSPs”) who share the Public Utility Commission of Texas’s (“Commission”) goals and
commend the Commission’s diligence in crafting a rule to fairly allocate transmission costs while
protecting residential customers, as the Legislature and Governor have instructed. To assist the
Commission, the Joint TSPs provide the below suggested modifications and clarifications to help
ensure the new rules avoid unintended incentives or consequences for utilities and customers.

       1. § 25.192(k): If interconnection fees and forfeited security will be required to be
             credited to retail customers, there are more efficient means to provide maximum
             benefit to customers from the credits, without creating financial risks to utilities.
             a. Any mechanism for crediting retail customers through contested ratemaking
                procedures would substantially delay the benefit to customers, increase rate-case
                expenses by adding to the number of issues to be resolved in rate cases, while also
                creating the likelihood of overpayments between rate cases. Additionally, applying

       1
           Proposal for Publication (Jul. 9, 2026) (“PFP”).

                                                          2
       these credits to rate base would eliminate the opportunity to earn a return on
      regulated investment.
   b. Similarly, applying such credits to a utility’s revenue requirement would
      unintentionally risk TSPs’ financial integrity. Particularly in the case of smaller
      TSPs, the credit being paid to retail customers may be higher than the utility’s
      revenues, resulting in a net deficit for the utility. A utility could be bankrupted by
      regulatory lag during the period between rate cases to implement and remove the
      offsets.
   c. Instead, fees and forfeited security could be credited annually to ERCOT-wide
      wholesale transmission costs as part of the transmission charge matrix proceeding
      typically approved in late Spring but effectively backdated to the beginning of each
      year. Such a mechanism would ensure that retail customers are credited in the most
      expeditious and transparent manner. Because the balance and credit may be
      changed from year to year in a single annual proceeding, it should impose the least
      administrative burden on the Commission and stakeholders and allow customers to
      realize these credits expeditiously without the incurrence of additional rate-case
      expenses.
   d. Alternatively, a credit rider might be applied outside of a TSP’s rate base or revenue
      requirement. This method ensures TSPs’ rates are based on actual costs, customers
      are timely and efficiently credited, and the process is transparent.
2. §§ 25.192(b)(13), (e)(6) and 25.252(b)(5): The Commission should clarify the term
   “transmission interconnection costs” in the proposed rule to avoid unintended
   impacts to utilities and customers. As drafted, the definition could be interpreted
   to broadly apply to any transmission customers, including generators or loads that
   are not considered large.
   a. “Transmission interconnection costs” should be limited to 1) the direct
      interconnection costs 2) to interconnect “large load customers” as defined in
      proposed 16 TAC § 25.194(c)(9), and 3) for which customers are required to pay a
      contribution in aid of construction (“CIAC”).
         Direct interconnection costs should be limited to 1) new radial lines or line
          upgrades, and 2) any necessary bay at the first station needed to interconnect
          the large load customer to the transmission system or upgrades to such bay.
         “Transmission interconnection costs” should not include interconnections for
          generators, Battery Electric Storage System (“BESS”) facilities, TSP-to-TSP,
          or TSP-to-distribution service provider (“DSP”) interconnections.



                                         3
                   “Transmission interconnection costs” should not include costs to interconnect
                   a transmission-level customer other than large load customers.
           b. PFP Question for Comment No. 5: The definition of “transmission interconnection
              costs” should not be broadened to include transmission projects that are
              recommended at the conclusion of a batch study.
                  No. Large loads compensate the grid for costs they impose through other
                   provisions in the rule, including CIAC, interconnection fees, minimum demand
                   charges, and financial security. Expanding the definition of “transmission
                   interconnection costs” to include projects recommended at the conclusion of a
                   batch study would create a double-recovery from these customers, who will
                   already be compensating the grid through CIAC and interconnection fees,
                   minimum demand charges, and forfeited financial securities.
                  Additionally, system upgrades are generally useful to the overall grid, and it is
                   not possible to verify any particular customer’s cost responsibility for such
                   upgrades.
       3. §§ 25.192(b)(7), (f)(1)(B) and 25.193(d): In determining the 12CP load, the
           proposed rules should refer to and incorporate the 20-year term for the large load
           minimum billing demand.
           a. The proposed rules should be revised to clarify that, for a DSP’s 12CP load or the
               ERCOT 12CP value used to calculate wholesale transmission rates, the minimum
               demand values would be incorporated for the required 20-year period so that the
               benefit will flow to all customers on the grid and to avoid other customers subsidizing
               the costs of the large loads.


                       II.      Comments on the Proposal for Publication

   1. § 25.192(k): If interconnection fees and forfeited security will be required to be
       credited to retail customers, there are more efficient means to provide maximum
       benefit to customers from the credits, without creating financial risks to utilities.

       Joint TSPs suggest that 16 § TAC 25.192(k) be revised to provide for a different method
of crediting interconnection fees and forfeited security to retail customers. Joint TSPs are
concerned that applying any such amounts as an offset to the TSP’s transmission revenue
requirement, as currently drafted, would result in a less efficient process to return those amounts
to retail customers. Additionally, Joint TSPs are concerned that utilizing the process as proposed
could create significant financial risks for utilities, as explained in more detail below.

                                                  4
        As mentioned, the proposed rule as currently drafted would require TSPs to offset their
transmission revenue requirement with any interconnection fees or forfeited security. That
provision would presumably require TSPs to file a general base rate case to effectuate the rule,
which is a time consuming and expensive process that would delay getting those dollars to retail
customers. Including these credits among a rate case’s many issues adds yet another issue to be
negotiated in a settlement or, alternatively, to be addressed by the presiding officer, resulting in
customers paying for rate-case expenses in order to receive the credits due to them.2
       As the Commission is aware, the filing of a base rate case generally takes at least six months
to prepare after the conclusion of a test year. Once a base rate case is on file, it usually takes at
least six months, if not longer, to implement those rates. As a result, returning any such amounts
to customers would take at least two years (one year for the test year, six months to prepare an
application, and six months for processing that application at the Commission). Furthermore, after
implementing those rates, a TSP would have to file another base rate case to remove any offsets
from its revenue requirement. This likely would result in a TSP continuing to credit its revenue
requirement and corresponding rates with offsets that have already been fully returned to
customers given the timeline just discussed with respect to preparing and processing a base rate
case application. Any mechanism to provide these amounts to customers should ensure that a TSP
does not have to provide amounts greater than what they receive from large loads. The proposed
rule, as currently drafted, would seem to place TSPs in that position based on the revenue
requirement offset mechanism.
       Additionally, Joint TSPs believe that the proposed rule poses serious financial risks to all
TSPs and, in particular, to the transmission-only utilities as they are generally the smallest
investor-owned utilities in Texas. For example, some of the total company revenue requirements
for the Joint TSPs range from approximately $50 million to approximately $100 million.
Nonetheless, interconnecting large load customers often seek to interconnect to these TSPs’
transmission facilities, including proposed loads exceeding one gigawatt (“GW”).                          As a
hypothetical, assume that a 2 GW customer paid a $100 million interconnection fee to the smallest
of the TSPs, with a revenue requirement that is slightly above $50 million. If the TSP were to
apply that $100 million as an offset to its revenue requirement through as base rate case, the TSP


       2
           See 16 TAC § 25.245 (Commission rule allowing for recovery of rate-case expenses from ratepayers).

                                                       5
 would have a negative revenue requirement and no cash flow for a period of approximately two
years until it was able to file and complete another base rate case to remove that offset. Having no
cash flow for an extended period of time would have serious financial risks and result in a
significant decline in credit metrics. In fact, one TSP with a revenue requirement of approximately
$75 million has already accepted over $600 million in financial security from large loads during
the Batch Zero process. While it is unlikely all of that financial security will be required to be
credited to customers, applying even a fraction of that amount as a credit to the utility’s revenue
requirement would create the financial predicament described above.
       Joint TSPs recognize that the revenue requirement offset concept is similar to how export
revenues are treated for TSPs. However, export revenues are generally limited to hundreds of
thousands of dollars as compared to potentially hundreds of millions of dollars. Thus, the impact
of offsetting the transmission revenue requirement with export revenue dollars does not have a
material financial impact on TSPs’ overall revenue requirements.
       Joint TSPs offer two alternatives to return any such amounts to retail customers that should
both address this concern and result in a timelier and more efficient method of providing any such
amounts to retail customers and would also lessen the financial risk to TSPs. First, interconnection
fees and forfeited security could be credited to DSPs, and ultimately retail customers, through the
annual proceeding to set wholesale transmission service charges for the ERCOT region. This
would entail TSPs providing any such interconnection fees and forfeited security to ERCOT who
could then credit the DSPs based on their load ratio share. DSPs could then distribute those
amounts to their retail customers. Joint TSPs believe that this would ensure any amounts are
allocated to customers in a timely and transparent manner and, at the same time, avoid a myriad
of base rate cases. Although typically approved in late Spring, the credit could be effectively
backdated to the beginning of each year, similar to how the Commission currently sets the 4CP
each year. Such a mechanism would ensure that retail customers are credited in the most
expeditious and transparent manner. Because the balance and credit may be changed from year to
year in a single annual proceeding, it also should impose the least administrative burden on the
Commission and allow customers to realize these credits without the incurrence of additional rate-
case expenses.
       Alternatively, the rule could provide for TSPs to file for a credit rider to provide
interconnection fees and forfeited security to customers. Joint TSPs believe that this method could


                                                 6
 involve a limited-issue tariff filing and avoid the burdensome nature of general base rate cases. It
also has the advantage of ensuring that TSPs do not have to return amounts greater than what they
receive given that TSPs can stop the credit rider once the specific amount has been returned. As
discussed above, a TSP could end up providing more than the amounts received given the timing
issues with filing and changing base rates. Additionally, this approach would avoid the potential
of eliminating a TSPs revenue requirement and would ensure that a TSP would still have cash flow
because the TSP would still be collecting its revenue requirement through base rates.

   2. §§ 25.192(b)(13), (e)(6) and 25.252(b)(5): The Commission should clarify the term
       “transmission interconnection costs” in the proposed rule to avoid unintended
       impacts to utilities. The term as currently drafted could be interpreted to broadly
       apply to any transmission customers, including generators or loads that are not
       considered large.

       To effectively and efficiently implement the Commission’s intention in adopting the
proposed rule, which the Joint TSPs understand is to ensure utilities do not obtain double recovery
of transmission plant already paid for through CIAC, the definition of “transmission
interconnection costs” should be clarified. As discussed below, Joint TSPs propose:
               The definition of “transmission interconnection costs” should be limited to 1) the
                direct interconnection costs 2) to interconnect “large load customers” as defined in
                proposed 16 TAC § 25.194(c)(9), and 3) for which customers are required to pay
                CIAC.

               The definition of “transmission interconnection costs” should not be broadened to
                include transmission projects that are recommended at the conclusion of a batch
                study. Instead, the “direct interconnection costs” discussed above should include
                only 1) new radial lines or line upgrades, and 2) any necessary bay at the first
                station needed to interconnect the large load customer, because these are the
                facilities that serve only the new interconnecting large loads.




                                                 7
               A. “Transmission interconnection costs” should be limited to 1) the direct
                  interconnection costs 2) to interconnect “large load customers” as defined in
                  proposed 16 TAC § 25.194(c)(9), and 3) for which customers are required to
                  pay CIAC.

        Clarification of the term “transmission interconnection costs” is needed to avoid
unintended consequences in the rule.             The currently proposed definition of “transmission
interconnection costs”3 includes all costs associated with the facilities required to physically
interconnect a transmission-level customer, without clarifying if that term is intended to include
or exclude interconnections for new generators, BESS facilities, or utility-to-utility
interconnections.4 Further, proposed 16 TAC § 25.192(e)(6) would remove all transmission
interconnection costs for new interconnections from utility cost of service, which could have
dramatic impacts on a utility’s rate base and financial integrity. If interpreted broadly, the
proposed rule also runs contrary to 16 TAC § 25.195(f), which requires that a TSP shall be
responsible for certain generator interconnection costs and therefore must recover such cost
through transmission rates.
        To remove ambiguity, Joint TSPs respectfully propose:
                  The “transmission interconnection costs” to be excluded from cost of service
                   should clearly be defined to include only 1) the direct interconnection costs 2) to
                   interconnect “large load customers” as defined in proposed 16 TAC § 25.194(c)(9),
                   and 3) for which customers are required to pay CIAC.

                  In limiting the definition to apply only to large load customer interconnections, the
                   Commission should clarify that “transmission interconnection costs” does not
                   include costs to interconnect a transmission-level customer other than large load
                   customers.




        3
            Proposed 16 TAC §§ 25.192(b)(13) and 25.252(b)(5).
        4
           See 16 TAC § 25.5(141) (defining “transmission service customer” to include a transmission service
provider, distribution service provider, river authority, municipally owned utility, electric cooperative, power
generation company, or exempt wholesale generator, among other entities, that is eligible to receive transmission
service). Conversely, a retail customer, such as a large load customer, is explicitly not a “transmission service
customer.” Id.

                                                       8
                 The direct interconnection costs referred to above should be limited to 1) new
                 radial lines or line upgrades, and 2) any necessary bay at the first station needed to
                 interconnect the large load customer to the transmission system or upgrades to such
                 bay, for the reasons discussed in Section II.2.B. below.

            B. PFP Question for Comment No. 5: The definition of “transmission
                interconnection costs” should not be broadened to include transmission
                projects that are recommended at the conclusion of a batch study.

        The definition of “transmission interconnection costs” to be recovered through CIAC and
excluded from cost of service should be limited to 1) new radial lines or line upgrades, and 2) any
necessary bay at the first station needed to interconnect the large load customer to the transmission
system or upgrades to such bay. These are the facilities that serve only the new interconnecting
large loads and are not attributable to any other user. The definition should not be broadened to
include system upgrades, including transmission projects that are recommended at the conclusion
of a batch study because:
                Large load customers compensate the grid for these system upgrades through other
                 provisions in the rule, including CIAC, interconnection fees, financial security, and
                 minimum billing demand charges,

                These system upgrades are generally useful to the overall grid, and

                It is not possible to verify any particular customer’s cost responsibility for such
                 upgrades.

        Expanding the definition of “transmission interconnection costs” to include projects
recommended at the conclusion of a batch study would create a double-recovery from large load
customers, who will already be compensating the grid through CIAC, interconnection fees,
potentially forfeited financial securities, and minimum billing demand charges. These provisions
already require cost recovery from large load developers in excess of the “direct” costs imposed.
A proposed interconnection fee of $50 thousand per megawatt, if applied to over 430 GW in
queue,5 would on its own recover more than $21.5 billion from large load developers. If the


         5
            ERCOT Interconnection and Grid Analysis Update (Jun. 2, 2026),                    available   at
https://www.ercot.com/files/docs/2026/05/24/8-Interconnection-and-Grid-Analysis-Update.pdf.

                                                    9
 Commission believes that additional contributions are needed to ensure lower costs for residential
customers, these bright-line cost recovery provisions should be adjusted instead.
        Additionally, broader system upgrades benefit the overall grid and may only incidentally
triggered by a new load. As such, the new load customer does not benefit to any greater degree
than any other transmission customer. The radial transmission line and any necessary bay at the
first station are considered in common industry practice to be the interconnection’s “direct” costs
and are attributable only to the interconnecting customer, and there are existing mechanisms to
charge these costs directly to the large load developer.
        Because the batch study process reviews several new interconnections simultaneously, it
will not be possible to specifically attribute network upgrades to a particular large load customer
or exclude any current customer. A bright-line rule limiting “transmission interconnection costs”
from being recovered through CIAC will reduce controversy and avoid unneeded litigation. A
clear definition also provides regulatory certainty for grid users and minimizes the potential for
under-recovery or stranded investment, fulfilling the Legislature’s charge to “support business
development in this state while minimizing the potential for stranded infrastructure costs.”6

    3. §§ 25.192(b)(7), (f)(1)(B) and 25.193(d): In determining the 12CP load, the proposed
        rules should refer to and incorporate the 20-year term for the large load minimum
        billing demand.

        The proposed rules should be revised to clarify that, in determining a DSP’s 12CP load or
the ERCOT 12CP value, any adjustment to account for the large load minimum billing demand
should refer to and incorporate the 20-year requirement. This would ensure that DSPs’ 12CP loads
used in setting wholesale transmission rates include the large load minimum billing demand for
the required 20-year period.
        This clarification ensures that the large load minimum billing demand inures to the benefit
of all customers for the entire 20-year period. Even if a large load facility ceases operations during
the 20-year period, DSPs must continue collecting the charge.7 While the charge is being collected,
the imputed billing units should continue to be included in the DSP’s 12CP load, so that the benefit

        6
            PURA § 37.0561(b).
        7
           Proposed 16 TAC § 25.193(d) (requiring DSPs to assess the large load minimum billing demand to Retail
Electric Providers for 20 years); proposed 16 TAC § 25.253(e) requiring DSPs’ tariffs to include the large load
minimum billing demand for 20 years).

                                                      10
 will flow to all customers on the grid. Otherwise, if the billing demand were not included for the
entire 20-year period, then the respective revenues would benefit only the DSP’s system, meaning
the large load’s costs would be subsidized by other customers.
       Joint TSPs respectfully propose that this change should be incorporated in proposed 16
TAC §§ 25.192(b)(7) and (f)(1)(B) and 25.193(d), as well as any other provisions where a DSP’s
12CP load may be impacted by the above.

                                       III.    Conclusion
       Joint TSPs appreciate the opportunity to contribute in this project and look forward to
working with Staff and stakeholders towards the effective implementation of SB 6’s requirements.

       Wind Energy Transmission Texas, LLC; Sharyland Utilities, L.L.C.; Cross Texas
Transmission, LLC, and Electric Transmission Texas, LLC (collectively, "Joint TSPs") jointly
submit these comments on the Proposal for Publication Amendments to 16 Tex. Admin. Code §§
25.192 and 25.193 ("TAC") and New 16 TAC § 25.252 ("PFP").l Perthe PFP, comments are due
August 11, 2026. Therefore, these comments are timely filed.

                                      I.       Executive Summary
       The Joint TSPs appreciate the opportunity to participate in the process of revising
transmission cost allocation and rate design in the Electric Reliability Council of Texas
( " ERCOT") area.     The Joint TSPs are all transmission-only transmission service providers
("TSPs") who share the Public Utility Commission of Texas' s ("Commission") goals and
commend the Commission's diligence in crafting a rule to fairly allocate transmission costs while
protecting residential customers, as the Legislature and Governor have instructed. To assist the
Commission, the Joint TSPs provide the below suggested modifications and clarifications to help
ensure the new rules avoid unintended incentives or consequences for utilities and customers.

       1. § 25.192(k): If interconnection fees and forfeited security will be required to be
           credited to retail customers, there are more efficient means to provide maximum
           benefit to customers from the credits, without creating financial risks to utilities.
           a. Any mechanism for crediting retail customers through contested ratemaking
              procedures would substantially delay the benefit to customers, increase rate-case
              expenses by adding to the number of issues to be resolved in rate cases, while also
              creating the likelihood of overpayments between rate cases. Additionally, applying

                       II.     Comments on the Proposal for Publication

    1. § 25.192(k): If interconnection fees and forfeited security will be required to be
       credited to retail customers, there are more efficient means to provide maximum
       benefit to customers from the credits, without creating financial risks to utilities.

       Joint TSPs suggest that 16 § TAC 25.192(k) be revised to provide for a different method
of crediting interconnection fees and forfeited security to retail customers.         Joint TSPs are
concerned that applying any such amounts as an offset to the TSP's transmission revenue
requirement, as currently drafted, would result in a less efficient process to return those amounts
to retail customers. Additionally, Joint TSPs are concerned that utilizing the process as proposed
could create significant financial risks for utilities, as explained in more detail below.

                                                  4
        As mentioned, the proposed rule as currently drafted would require TSPs to offset their
transmission revenue requirement with any interconnection fees or forfeited security.                    That
provision would presumably require TSPs to file a general base rate case to effectuate the rule,
which is a time consuming and expensive process that would delay getting those dollars to retail
customers. Including these credits among a rate case' s many issues adds yet another issue to be
negotiated in a settlement or, alternatively, to be addressed by the presiding officer, resulting in
customers paying for rate-case expenses in order to receive the credits due to them.2
       As the Commission is aware, the filing of a base rate case generally takes at least six months
to prepare after the conclusion of a test year. Once a base rate case is on file, it usually takes at
least six months, if not longer, to implement those rates. As a result, returning any such amounts
to customers would take at least two years (one year for the test year, six months to prepare an
application, and six months for processing that application at the Commission). Furthermore, after
implementing those rates, a TSP would have to file another base rate case to remove any offsets
from its revenue requirement. This likely would result in a TSP continuing to credit its revenue
requirement and corresponding rates with offsets that have already been fully returned to
customers given the timeline just discussed with respect to preparing and processing a base rate
case application. Any mechanism to provide these amounts to customers should ensure that a TSP
does not have to provide amounts greater than what they receive from large loads. The proposed
rule, as currently drafted, would seem to place TSPs in that position based on the revenue
requirement offset mechanism.
       Additionally, Joint TSPs believe that the proposed rule poses serious financial risks to all
TSPs and, in particular, to the transmission-only utilities as they are generally the smallest
investor-owned utilities in Texas. For example, some of the total company revenue requirements
for the Joint TSPs range from approximately $50 million to approximately $100 million.
Nonetheless, interconnecting large load customers often seek to interconnect to these TSPs'
transmission facilities, including proposed loads exceeding one gigawatt ("GW").                        As a
hypothetical, assume that a 2 GW customer paid a $100 million interconnection fee to the smallest
of the TSPs, with a revenue requirement that is slightly above $50 million. If the TSP were to
apply that $100 million as an offset to its revenue requirement through as base rate case, the TSP

 would have a negative revenue requirement and no cash flow for a period of approximately two
years until it was able to file and complete another base rate case to remove that offset. Having no
cash flow for an extended period of time would have serious financial risks and result in a
significant decline in credit metrics. In fact, one TSP with a revenue requirement of approximately
$75 million has already accepted over $600 million in financial security from large loads during
the Batch Zero process. While it is unlikely all of that financial security will be required to be
credited to customers, applying even a fraction of that amount as a credit to the utility' s revenue
requirement would create the financial predicament described above.
       Joint TSPs recognize that the revenue requirement offset concept is similar to how export
revenues are treated for TSPs. However, export revenues are generally limited to hundreds of
thousands of dollars as compared to potentially hundreds of millions of dollars. Thus, the impact
of offsetting the transmission revenue requirement with export revenue dollars does not have a
material financial impact on TSPs' overall revenue requirements.
       Joint TSPs offer two alternatives to return any such amounts to retail customers that should
both address this concern and result in a timelier and more efficient method of providing any such
amounts to retail customers and would also lessen the financial risk to TSPs. First, interconnection
fees and forfeited security could be credited to DSPs, and ultimately retail customers, through the
annual proceeding to set wholesale transmission service charges for the ERCOT region. This
would entail TSPs providing any such interconnection fees and forfeited security to ERCOT who
could then credit the DSPs based on their load ratio share. DSPs could then distribute those
amounts to their retail customers. Joint TSPs believe that this would ensure any amounts are
allocated to customers in a timely and transparent manner and, at the same time, avoid a myriad
of base rate cases. Although typically approved in late Spring, the credit could be effectively
backdated to the beginning of each year, similar to how the Commission currently sets the 4CP
each year.   Such a mechanism would ensure that retail customers are credited in the most
expeditious and transparent manner. Because the balance and credit may be changed from year to
year in a single annual proceeding, it also should impose the least administrative burden on the
Commission and allow customers to realize these credits without the incurrence of additional rate-
case expenses.
       Alternatively, the rule could provide for TSPs to file for a credit rider to provide
interconnection fees and forfeited security to customers. Joint TSPs believe that this method could


                                                 6
 involve a limited-issue tariff filing and avoid the burdensome nature of general base rate cases. It
also has the advantage of ensuring that TSPs do not have to return amounts greater than what they
receive given that TSPs can stop the credit rider once the specific amount has been returned. As
discussed above, a TSP could end up providing more than the amounts received given the timing
issues with filing and changing base rates. Additionally, this approach would avoid the potential
of eliminating a TSPs revenue requirement and would ensure that a TSP would still have cash flow
because the TSP would still be collecting its revenue requirement through base rates.

            B. PFP Question for Comment No. 5: The definition of "transmission
                 interconnection costs" should not be broadened to include transmission
                 projects that are recommended at the conclusion of a batch study.

        The definition of"transmission interconnection costs" to be recovered through CIAC and
excluded from cost of service should be limited to 1) new radial lines or line upgrades, and 2) any
necessary bay at the first station needed to interconnect the large load customer to the transmission
system or upgrades to such bay. These are the facilities that serve only the new interconnecting
large loads and are not attributable to any other user. The definition should not be broadened to
include system upgrades, including transmission projects that are recommended at the conclusion
of a batch study because:
             •   Large load customers compensate the grid for these system upgrades through other
                 provisions in the rule, including CIAC, interconnection fees, financial security, and
                 minimum billing demand charges,

             •   These system upgrades are generally useful to the overall grid, and

             •   It is not possible to verify any particular customer's cost responsibility for such
                 upgrades.

        Expanding the definition of "transmission interconnection costs" to include projects
recommended at the conclusion of a batch study would create a double-recovery from large load
customers, who will already be compensating the grid through CIAC, interconnection fees,
potentially forfeited financial securities, and minimum billing demand charges. These provisions
already require cost recovery from large load developers in excess of the "direct" costs imposed.
A proposed interconnection fee of $50 thousand per megawatt, if applied to over 430 GW in
queue, 5 would on its own recover more than $21.5 billion from large load developers. If the

 Commission believes that additional contributions are needed to ensure lower costs for residential
customers, these bright-line cost recovery provisions should be adjusted instead.
        Additionally, broader system upgrades benefit the overall grid and may only incidentally
triggered by a new load. As such, the new load customer does not benefit to any greater degree
than any other transmission customer. The radial transmission line and any necessary bay at the
first station are considered in common industry practice to be the interconnection' s "direct" costs
and are attributable only to the interconnecting customer, and there are existing mechanisms to
charge these costs directly to the large load developer.
        Because the batch study process reviews several new interconnections simultaneously, it
will not be possible to specifically attribute network upgrades to a particular large load customer
or exclude any current customer. A bright-line rule limiting "transmission interconnection costs"
from being recovered through CIAC will reduce controversy and avoid unneeded litigation. A
clear definition also provides regulatory certainty for grid users and minimizes the potential for
under-recovery or stranded investment, fulfilling the Legislature' s charge to "support business
development in this state while minimizing the potential for stranded infrastructure costs."6

    3. §§ 25.192(b)(7), (f)(1)(B) and 25.193(d): In determining the 12CP load, the proposed
        rules should refer to and incorporate the 20-year term for the large load minimum
        billing demand.

        The proposed rules should be revised to clarify that, in determining a DSP' s 12CP load or
the ERCOT 12CP value, any adjustment to account for the large load minimum billing demand
should refer to and incorporate the 20-year requirement. This would ensure that DSPs' 12CP loads
used in setting wholesale transmission rates include the large load minimum billing demand for
the required 20-year period.
        This clarification ensures that the large load minimum billing demand inures to the benefit
of all customers for the entire 20-year period. Even if a large load facility ceases operations during
the 20-year period, DSPs must continue collecting the charge.7 While the charge is being collected,
the imputed billing units should continue to be included in the DSP' s 12CP load, so that the benefit
